summary: Bosnia and Herzegovina lets citizens of the EU, EEA and most countries on the EU visa-free list — plus Russia, Turkey, China and the Gulf states — visit visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180 (30 days for Russians and Ukrainians), while other travelers need a short-stay visa from a Bosnian embassy or can enter for up to 30 days with a valid multiple-entry Schengen visa.

notes: Duty-free allowances broadly follow European norms (200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits). Declare anything beyond personal use.
Taking convertible marks (BAM) out of the country is pointless. The currency is essentially non-exchangeable abroad, so spend or exchange before leaving.

payments.text: The convertible mark is pegged to the euro at 1.95583 KM. Cards work in city hotels, supermarkets and most Sarajevo and Mostar restaurants, but keep cash for cafés, taxis, markets and anywhere rural — euros are often informally accepted for round sums.

safety.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina is safe for visitors, with low violent crime. The serious residual risk is landmines from the 1990s war in remote rural areas. Stay on paved roads and marked trails and heed warning signs. Petty theft occurs in Sarajevo's tourist areas.

bestTimeToVisit.text: May–September is best for Sarajevo, Mostar and rafting on the Neretva and Una rivers; winter brings inexpensive skiing on the 1984 Olympic mountains of Jahorina and Bjelašnica.

idp.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Bosnia and Herzegovina yet.

tips.text: Unexploded landmines from the 1990s war remain in remote rural and mountain areas. Stick to paved roads, marked trails and well-trodden paths, and never touch suspicious objects or enter taped-off areas.

Your stay must be registered with the authorities within 48 hours of arrival. Hotels do it automatically; if you are staying in a private apartment, make sure your host registers you — checks can happen on departure.
Carry convertible marks (KM) in cash outside the main cities. Many cafés, taxis and rural guesthouses do not take cards, and KM cannot realistically be exchanged once you leave the country.
If you hold a valid multiple-entry Schengen visa, you can enter Bosnia and Herzegovina without a Bosnian visa for up to 30 days — a common route for visa-required nationalities touring the Balkans.
Bosnia and Herzegovina is not in the EU or Schengen, so days spent there do not count against your Schengen 90/180 allowance — useful when combining it with Croatia.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Bosnia and Herzegovina?
faq.answer: Most Western travelers do not: citizens of the EU, EEA, US, UK, Canada, Australia and the other countries on the EU visa-free list can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period, and EU/EEA citizens can enter with just an ID card. Russia and Ukraine get 30 days per visit; Turkey, China and the Gulf states get 90 days. Everyone else needs a short-stay visa from a Bosnian mission.

faq.question: Can I enter Bosnia and Herzegovina with a Schengen visa?
faq.answer: Yes — holders of a valid multiple-entry Schengen visa can enter visa-free for up to 30 days (within the visa's validity), without applying for a Bosnian visa. Single-entry visas do not qualify; confirm details with a Bosnian mission before travel.

faq.question: What currency is used in Bosnia and Herzegovina?
faq.answer: The convertible mark (BAM, written KM), pegged to the euro at 1.95583 KM per euro. Cards are fine in city establishments, but carry cash elsewhere, and spend or exchange your marks before leaving, as they are hard to exchange abroad.

faq.question: Is Bosnia and Herzegovina safe to visit?
faq.answer: Yes — cities like Sarajevo and Mostar are safe, with low violent crime. The one serious hazard is leftover landmines in remote rural areas: stay on paved roads and marked trails, and heed local warning signs when hiking.

faq.question: Do days in Bosnia count against the Schengen 90/180 limit?
faq.answer: No. Bosnia and Herzegovina is outside the EU and Schengen, so time spent there does not use up your Schengen allowance — many long-term travelers alternate between Croatia and Bosnia for this reason.
